result:
I've been thinking about lichen.

Not because anyone asked. It's just that lichen is one of those things that, once you notice it, turns out to be everywhere: the pale green crust on a gravestone, the orange splash on a seaside rock, the grey-green beards hanging off spruce branches in wet forests. It's so ordinary that it becomes invisible, and so strange that it shouldn't be.

Lichen isn't a plant. It isn't one organism at all. It's a fungus that has taken in an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium, or both) and built a body around it. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral scavenging; the alga photosynthesizes and pays rent in sugar. Neither could live where the lichen lives on its own. The fungus can't make food from light; the alga would dry out and blow away. Together they colonize bare rock, Antarctic valleys, the sides of highway overpasses. Some have survived exposure to open space and come back fine.

What I find interesting is that the arrangement is old enough and stable enough that lichens have names. Taxonomists gave them species designations for two centuries before anyone realized each "species" was really a partnership. And the names stuck, because the partnership behaves like a thing. It has a shape. It reproduces. It has a characteristic color and a preferred habitat. The fact that it is two lineages, evolutionarily distant, acting as one body—this turns out not to matter much for describing what it does in the world.

They are also, famously, slow. Some map lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on rocks in Scandinavia that are thought to be several thousand years old, which means a single organism-that-is-two-organisms has been sitting on the same stone since before the alphabet. It has weathered everything from the Bronze Age onward by doing almost nothing: holding on, absorbing a little moisture, dissolving a few molecules of rock, and waiting.

I don't want to turn lichen into a metaphor too quickly. It's tempting—the collaboration, the resilience, the patience—but the metaphor is less interesting than the thing itself. A lichen doesn't know it's collaborating. It isn't patient; it just has a metabolism that works at a certain pace. The lesson, if there is one, is not "be like lichen." It's something closer to: the categories we bring to the world are provisional, and the world doesn't owe them anything. We wanted organisms to be individuals with clear boundaries. Lichen shrugged.

There's a phrase I like from a lichenologist, Trevor Goward: "Lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture." It's a joke, but it's a good joke, because it reframes the fungus from passive host into something with a strategy. It grows its own crops. It just does it on a timescale and in a body plan that we didn't have a word for.

Next time you're outside, look at a rock or a tree trunk or an old fence. There's a decent chance something is living there that is two things pretending to be one, that has been there longer than you've been alive, and that will outlast the fence. It's not doing anything you'd call dramatic. It's just quietly refusing to fit the categories we made for it, and thriving anyway.
